entities.name: Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum (Państwowe Muzeum Auschwitz-Birkenau), established in 1947 on the site of the Nazi German concentration and extermination camps of Auschwitz I and Auschwitz II-Birkenau where approximately 1.1 million people were murdered (90% Jewish, along with Polish political prisoners, Roma, Soviet POWs, and others), is the most visited Holocaust memorial and museum in the world — with approximately 1.5-2 million visitors annually — and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979 designated as a site of exceptional universal significance.

Auschwitz was the largest single site of the Holocaust: its gas chambers and crematoria killed more people than any other single location in human history in the modern era. The museum's preserved buildings — the entry gate with its cynical 'Arbeit Macht Frei' ('Work makes you free') inscription, the rows of brick barracks, the ruins of the Birkenau crematoria dynamited by retreating SS, the victims' belongings (suitcases, shoes, hair, eyeglasses) displayed in Block 4 — constitute one of the most powerful architectural testimonies to human evil ever preserved.

The museum's mission — 'to preserve the authentic historical site' and 'to document the history of Auschwitz' — faces ongoing challenges: the wooden Birkenau barracks are deteriorating, the authentic evidence is fragile, and the volume of visitors requires careful management. The museum has been central to Holocaust education worldwide, training teachers and hosting school groups; the 'Arbeit Macht Frei' gate was stolen and recovered in 2009. As the last Auschwitz survivors age, the museum's role in Holocaust memory is transitioning from living testimony to institutional memory.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum — the memorial to the 20th century's most devastating genocide, the most-visited Holocaust site, preserving authentic evidence of humanity's greatest evil, and the world's most important institution of Holocaust memory — is among the most historically significant sites and institutions on Earth.
